# The hull of two intervals, one-limb bounds

<!-- Generated by docs/tools/reference.py from gen/claims.json, gen/kernels/, include/kairn/gen/bounds.hpp, proofs/gen/, proofs/audit/, results/milestone2/brute/ and docs/tools/reference_operations.py. Do not edit: run python3 docs/tools/reference.py. -->

Kernel `interval_hull_1` · proved · [all operations](index.md) · [how to read this page](reading.md)

## What it computes

The hull of two intervals, the smallest interval that contains both, exactly; the empty set included:

$$Z = \mathrm{hull}(X \cup Y).$$

## C++

| Form | Operands | Result | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `X.hull(Y)` | `Interval<T, 1>`, `Interval<T, 1>` | `Interval<T, 1>` | `constexpr`; does not round |

`T` is `float` or `double`; the operations are in namespace `kairn`, header `kairn/kairn.hpp`. The operators and functions also accept the marker `kairn::unverified` on an operand, which they need while the kernel is UNVERIFIED.

## Requires

- $X = [x_l, x_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $x_l = +\infty$ and $x_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $x_l \le x_u$, $x_l < +\infty$, $x_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.
- $Y = [y_l, y_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $y_l = +\infty$ and $y_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $y_l \le y_u$, $y_l < +\infty$, $y_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.

## Guarantees

For operands that satisfy the requirements, finite, infinite or NaN:

- The result $Z = [z_l, z_u]$ is a canonical interval.
- $Z$ is empty exactly when $X$ and $Y$ both are.
- Otherwise $Z$ is the smallest interval that contains $X \cup Y$, exactly: its lower bound is the smaller of the lower bounds of the nonempty operands, its upper bound the larger of their upper bounds ($[z_l, z_u]$ with $\min(x_l, y_l)$ and $\max(x_u, y_u)$ when both are nonempty); the hull with the empty set is the other operand.

Proved for every binary format with a precision of at least 1 bit, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Status

**Proved.** Rocq checks the theorem `interval_hull_1_correct`, in [`proofs/theories/IeeeIntervalExact.v`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/theories/IeeeIntervalExact.v); the audit of `make -C proofs` prints the axioms its proof depends on (`Print Assumptions interval_hull_1_correct`, in [`proofs/gen/IeeeAudit.v`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/gen/IeeeAudit.v)) and finds none beyond the four allowed ([Axioms](#axioms)).

## Axioms

The audit accepts a proof only if every axiom it depends on is one of the four listed in [`proofs/audit/allowed_axioms.txt`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/audit/allowed_axioms.txt) ([Proofs](../proofs/index.md#the-four-axioms) says what each states):

- `ClassicalDedekindReals.sig_forall_dec`
- `ClassicalDedekindReals.sig_not_dec`
- `FunctionalExtensionality.functional_extensionality_dep`
- `Classical_Prop.classic`

Which of them the proof of `interval_hull_1_correct` depends on is not copied here: only a run of Rocq computes it. The CI prints it for every push to `main` and every pull request, and keeps what the audit printed as the artifact `proof-audit` of each run of the [Proofs workflow](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/actions/workflows/proofs.yml).

## Source

**Algorithm:** the smaller lower bound and the larger upper bound (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/interval_hull_1.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/interval_hull_1.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal model (`proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).

```
# The hull of two intervals with one-limb bounds (milestone2.md, "One enclosure interface"): the
# smaller lower bound and the larger upper bound, exact. No test of emptiness: the empty set is
# stored as (+inf, -inf), so the hull with it is the other operand, and of two empty sets the empty
# set (milestone2.md, "Values of an interval"). The bounds are canonical, so no comparison sees a
# NaN. For every precision.

ml = lt(yl, xl)
zl = select(ml, yl, xl)
mu = lt(xu, yu)
zu = select(mu, yu, xu)
```

## Measured

The latest brute-force runs, from the stored summaries in [`results/milestone2/brute/`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/tree/main/results/milestone2/brute) ([the report](../developer/results/brute-milestone2.md#interval_hull_1)): the oracle judged, in exact arithmetic, the results of the compiled kernel (every compiler, scalar and packed code, every contraction setting) on random operands of `binary64` and `binary32`, and those of the generator's interpreter on every operand of small formats. A measurement, not a bound.
They judged the kernel in the extended domain, infinite and NaN operands included, as the oracle reads its statement in the IEEE model ([Claims of the non-finite layer](../developer/architecture.md#claims-of-the-non-finite-layer)).

| Run | Cases judged | Failed |
|---|---|---|
| `binary64` (`double`), compiled: 90 runners on 3 machines | 7 200 000 | 0 |
| `binary32` (`float`), compiled: 90 runners on 3 machines | 7 200 000 | 0 |
| toy formats, every operand: 5 domains of 5 formats | 4 740 377 | 0 |

## Not claimed

- Anything for operands that do not satisfy the requirements.
- The sign of a zero limb, and which NaN a NaN result is: the claims compare neither.
